title: Combinatorics Basics
tagline: Counting with permutations, combinations, and Pascal — plus nCr mod p at scale.

intuition.analogy: Choosing a 3-person committee from 10 people: order doesn't matter, so you count arrangements (10·9·8) then divide out the orderings of the chosen 3 (3!). That's exactly C(10,3).
paragraphs: Combinatorics is the art of counting without enumerating. The two pillars are permutations P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)! (order matters) and combinations C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!) (order doesn't).

Pascal's rule C(n,k)=C(n−1,k−1)+C(n−1,k) builds the triangle and underlies many DP recurrences (paths in a grid, subsets of a size). Recognising a problem as 'choose k of n' often collapses it instantly.

For large n under a prime modulus, precompute factorials and inverse factorials once, then C(n,k)=fact[n]·invfact[k]·invfact[n−k] mod p answers each query in O(1) — the standard competitive-programming setup.
intuition.keyIdea: Permutations count ordered choices, combinations unordered; precompute factorials + inverses for O(1) nCr mod p.

steps.title: Permutations vs combinations
steps.detail: P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!; C(n,k)=P(n,k)/k!. Decide whether order matters.

steps.title: Pascal's triangle
steps.detail: C(n,k)=C(n−1,k−1)+C(n−1,k); useful for small n or DP transitions.

steps.title: nCr mod p
steps.detail: Precompute fact[] and invfact[] (invfact[n]=power(fact[n], p−2)); then C(n,k)=fact[n]·invfact[k]·invfact[n−k] mod p.

complexity.timeReason: Factorials and one inverse computed once; each query is constant.

pitfalls: Compute invfact in reverse from a single inverse to avoid n log p inversions.
C(n,k)=0 when k<0 or k>n — guard the bounds.
Watch overflow: reduce mod after every multiplication.

dryRun.clickMoment: Both routes agree on 10: the formula 5·4/2! and Pascal's C(4,1)+C(4,2). Seeing them match cements why 'choose' divides out the orderings.
